feedback: If a learner lists parts with no function, prompt for each: 'What job does it do?' — compound eyes = wide/motion vision; spiracles = breathing holes; proboscis = drinking. Tie every part to a function before moving on.

If a learner says the insect breathes through its mouth, show the row of spiracles down the body — air goes in there, not the mouth — and contrast with the human nose and lungs to make the difference explicit.
If a learner thinks compound eyes work like our single-lens eyes, revisit the drill-down into the lens array and the mosaic view to show many lenses rather than one.
activities.intendedInsight: Each specialised insect structure exists because of the job it does: mouthparts match diet, spiracles enable breathing under a rigid exoskeleton, and compound eyes are arrays of many lenses — not single-lens eyes like ours.
learnerActions: Study a strongly magnified, highly detailed insect image so tiny structures (lenses, spiracles) are actually visible.

Examine the bulging eye, zoomed in until its surface resolves into many tiny hexagonal lenses (thousands in insects such as flies and dragonflies); compare a mosaic 'insect-vision' view of the world and describe why many lenses pointing in different directions help spot movement quickly across a wide view, even though the picture is less sharp than ours.
Examine the mouth across a beetle (crunching mandibles), a butterfly (coiled drinking-straw proboscis) and a fly (sponging pad); for each, pair it with the food it is built for.
Find the small spiracles dotted along the body and state that air enters there, along the body, not through the mouth.
Confront the puzzle posed by the shell: 'if your skeleton is on the OUTSIDE, how do you grow?' then view a moult sequence of the insect wriggling out of its old casing.
For each structure, state in one sentence the job it does before moving on.
activities.title: Explore a magnified insect: each part and the job it does

feedback: If a learner treats mouthparts as interchangeable (any insect could eat any food if it tried), make structure a constraint: a coiled straw cannot cut and jaws cannot reach deep into a flower. Match each real mouthpart to what it physically can and cannot do, using the straw-versus-pliers analogy.

If a learner says the exoskeleton grows with the insect or that insects grow continuously like us, revisit the moult: the old casing is shed because a hardened shell cannot expand much, and the new soft shell stretches larger before hardening, so the insect's outer size increases in steps.

Correct answer to the beetle/butterfly comparison: their mouthparts differ because they eat different foods and each mouthpart suits its food. The beetle chews solid food (leaves, other insects) so it needs hard jaws; the adult butterfly drinks liquid nectar from deep in flowers so it needs a long thin tube to reach and suck it up. An adult butterfly could NOT eat a leaf like a beetle: its proboscis is a drinking straw, not a cutting tool, so it can only take liquids (its caterpillar, by contrast, has chewing jaws and does eat leaves). Structure matches function.
activities.intendedInsight: Form constrains what an animal can do: mouthparts are not interchangeable, and a rigid exoskeleton forces stepwise growth by moulting.
learnerActions: Match each mouthpart to the food it is built for: proboscis → nectar, mandibles → leaf, sponging pad → spilled liquid.
Explain why the match works using tool analogies: a coiled straw can suck but cannot cut; jaws can cut but cannot reach deep into a flower.
Reason about a constraint: could an adult butterfly eat a leaf the way a beetle does? Explain why not.

Trigger a moult sequence as the insect outgrows its shell, and explain that the insect's outer size increases in steps because the hard exoskeleton cannot stretch much and must be shed and replaced — the new, soft exoskeleton expands before it hardens; the old one does not grow with the insect.
activities.title: Match the mouthpart to its food, and moult to grow

feedback: If a learner only recalls studied examples, prompt them to reason from the shape of a new structure to its job, then to the food it suits — a thin, sharp, needle-like tube can pierce skin or a plant stem and then suck, suggesting the insect feeds on liquids inside, such as blood or plant sap.
For biomimicry, accept any answer that names a real insect structure and a plausible technology it could inspire, and that explains the shared function linking them.
activities.intendedInsight: Structure-function reasoning transfers: you can predict an insect's diet from an unfamiliar mouthpart, and the same principle explains why engineers copy insect designs.
learnerActions: Given a new structure not studied directly (for example a mosquito's or aphid's needle-like piercing-sucking mouthparts), infer the kind of food the insect eats and explain the reasoning.

Give one example of biomimicry where human technology is inspired by an insect structure or ability, pairing the structure with the design (for example compound eye → camera array; exoskeleton → body armour or robotics).
Pick one insect structure and propose what it might inspire in engineering or design, explaining the shared function.
activities.title: Infer function from an unfamiliar structure, and explore biomimicry
